content: Carotenoderma, also known as carotenemia, carotenaemia, or hypercarotenemia, is a condition characterized by a yellowish or orange discoloration of the skin. This discoloration is most commonly observed on the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet and is caused by elevated levels of carotene in the body. It is frequently seen in individuals who follow vegetarian diets. In infants and young children, the discoloration is often most noticeable on the skin of the nose. This condition, also referred to as xanthosis cutis, is both reversible and harmless. Carotenoderma typically occurs when an individual consumes chronic doses of carotenoids exceeding 30 mg per day. This is most often due to the excessive intake of carotene-rich foods, such as carrots. While all pigmented fruits and vegetables contain some amount of carotene, particularly high concentrations are found in breast milk, carrots, squash, sweet potatoes, pumpkin, spinach, beans, egg yolks, corn, and yams. Aside from the yellowish discoloration of the skin, carotenoderma does not present with any significant symptoms or toxicity. It is important to note that this is not the case for vitamin A, which the liver can convert from carotene. Excessive vitamin A can lead to toxicity, unlike carotene. The most common cause of carotenoderma is the overconsumption of carotene-rich foods. However, it can also be a clinical sign of underlying medical conditions, including anorexia nervosa, diabetes mellitus, hepatic diseases, hyperlipidemia, hypothyroidism, porphyria, and renal diseases. Infants and young children are particularly susceptible to carotenoderma due to their consumption of cooked, mashed, and pureed vegetables. The processing and homogenization of these foods increase the bioavailability of carotene, making it easier for the body to absorb. For example, a 5-ounce jar of baby food containing sweet potatoes or carrots can provide 400-500% of an infant's recommended daily value of carotene. Additionally, infants are often prescribed liquid vitamin supplements, such as Tri-Vi-Sol, which contain vitamin A. The diagnosis of carotenoderma is primarily based on physical examination, with the yellowish discoloration of the skin being the hallmark feature. This condition is often documented in dermatology atlases as carotenaemia. Carotenoderma itself is harmless and does not require medical treatment. The discoloration of the skin will gradually return to normal once the excessive intake of carotene is discontinued. However, this process may take several months. In the case of infants, prescribed vitamin supplements should not be discontinued unless specifically advised by a pediatrician. If carotenoderma is associated with an underlying medical disorder, treatment should focus on addressing the root cause. Many fruits and vegetables contain carotene, with carrots being the most notable source. Similar conditions can occur due to the excessive consumption of other plant pigments. For example, lycopenodermia, caused by the overconsumption of lycopene (a pigment found in tomatoes), can result in a deep orange discoloration of the skin. Like carotenoderma, lycopenodermia is harmless. Another condition, argyria, occurs when there is excessive consumption or exposure to elemental silver, silver dust, or silver compounds, leading to a bluish or bluish-gray discoloration of the skin.
